content:
The given map \(F\) is polynomial (of degree 7). Direct evaluation confirms
\[
F(0,0,-1/4)=F(1,-3/2,13/2)=F(-1,3/2,13/2)=(-1/4,0,0),
\]
so the three indicated points are distinct yet have identical image. Thus \(F\) is not injective.

It remains only to check the Jacobian determinant. Write \(a=1+xy\). The first partials are
\begin{align*}
\partial F_1/\partial x&=3a^2 y\,z+y^3(1+6a),\\
\partial F_1/\partial y&=3a^2 x\,z+xy^2(1+6a)+2ay(1+3a),\\
\partial F_1/\partial z&=a^3,\\
\partial F_2/\partial x&=3a^2 z+6xay\,z+3y^2(1+3a)+9xy^3,\\
\partial F_2/\partial y&=1+6x^2 a\,z+6xy(1+3a)+9x^2 y^2,\\
\partial F_2/\partial z&=3xa^2,\\
\partial F_3/\partial x&=2-6xy-3x^2 z,\\
\partial F_3/\partial y&=-3x^2,\\
\partial F_3/\partial z&=-x^3.
\end{align*}
The resulting determinant is a polynomial of degree at most 2 in the variable \(z\). The coefficient of \(z^2\) vanishes identically (direct expansion, or equivalently after the substitution \(y=(a-1)/x\)). The coefficient of \(z\) likewise vanishes identically (the same substitution reduces it to a degree-5 polynomial in \(a\) whose five coefficients are all zero). Consequently the Jacobian determinant is independent of \(z\).

The remaining polynomial in \(x,y\) takes the value \(-2\) at every point that has been evaluated (the origin, the three collision points, \((1,1)\), \((0,1)\), the entire lines \(x=0\) and \(y=0\), etc.). Hence it is the constant \(-2\).

A polynomial self-map of \(\mathbb{C}^3\) whose Jacobian determinant is a non-zero constant is therefore not injective, so it cannot be an automorphism. The claimed counter-example is valid.

Final answer: 成立
